texto:
Walmart on October 21, 2026, set out three pieces of infrastructure for artificial intelligence agents that shop for its customers: Agent Profiles, the Walmart Agent Gateway and a set of terms that agents must follow on Walmart and Sam's Club. The post, published on the Walmart corporate newsroom without a named author, describes a dedicated profile for each agent inside a customer's account, optional spending limits, a faster machine-to-machine route for agents and a rule that agents which break the terms will be blocked from Walmart's site. A separate, undated beta page on Walmart.com invites agent builders to request access to the gateway, which it describes as an early, invitation-only program.
In Short
Walmart is building a special door for AI shopping helpers, so the helper gets its own login inside your account instead of borrowing yours. You can make it ask before every purchase or let it spend up to a limit you pick, and you can see everything it bought in one place. Helpers that break Walmart's rules will be shut out, and the helper never gets your card number.
What Walmart announced
The newsroom post opens with company history before reaching the product. Walmart lists the places it already sells: stores and clubs, online shopping, pickup and delivery, and "Sparky and conversational commerce integrations with Muse, ChatGPT, Gemini and others." Sparky is Walmart's own shopping assistant. Muse is the consumer agent Meta released in September 2026.
The core of the announcement is a sentence that names all three components at once. "That's why we're introducing Agent Profiles, the Walmart Agent Gateway and terms for AI agents," according to Walmart. "Together, these tools will let customers shop with Walmart and Sam's Club through the apps and agents they choose, with clear permissions, controls and protections built in."
Walmart was also careful to frame the scope. "Shopping with an agent won't be for everyone, and it doesn't have to be," the post states. The company's stated goal for those who do use one is "to make our experience the most trusted by building clear controls and protections into the experience from the start."
The problem Walmart describes
According to Walmart, an AI agent that shops today signs in with the customer's own credentials. The consequence, in the post's words: "all purchases - whether made by the customer or the agent - appear together, without any differentiation." A household cannot tell from its order history which items a person chose and which a piece of software chose.
The second problem is mechanical. "Today, agents may shop on Walmart's site through a web browser, following steps designed for people," according to Walmart. "This can be slow and error-prone, and agents may get stuck along the way." The website, the company notes, is built for people who browse, click and sign in themselves.
Agent Profiles
Agent Profiles are scheduled to launch "in the next month," according to the post, which points to a launch by late November 2026, in the run-up to the holiday peak. No exact date is given.
Each authorised agent receives a dedicated profile inside the customer's Walmart account. Purchases made by the agent then appear separately from the customer's own purchases. Customers choose one of two approval models: approval for every purchase, or permission for the agent to buy within a spending limit the customer sets. Walmart gives "$50, $100 or $200" as examples. Those figures are illustrations in the post, not fixed tiers, and Walmart does not say whether the limit applies per order, per day or per month.
The company reaches for a familiar comparison. Giving an agent a profile, the post says, is like "adding someone as a cardholder on your credit card," where the account holder sets a limit and tracks use. The difference is that the agent gets "its own profile to shop, with permissions and spending limits set by the customer and the ability to turn them off at any time."
How a profile is created
The post sets out a three-step flow:
- Start in the agent's app. The first time an agent shops through the Walmart Agent Gateway, Walmart automatically creates an Agent Profile for that agent.
- Connect through Walmart. The customer authorises and links the profile by signing in to their Walmart account. "Only Walmart sees this," according to the post.
- Set controls. The customer picks a spending limit, sees purchases from every agent, and can delete an Agent Profile at any time.
That sequence matters. Profiles are generated by the gateway, so an agent that keeps shopping through a web browser with the customer's password would not, on the post's description, receive one. The beta page reinforces the link: "Your agent shops through a separate Agent Profile."
Pricing
The post includes a pricing commitment. "We price products, not people, so the prices that an AI agent sees are the same prices that a human would see on Walmart.com, with applicable offers and fees shown before purchase," according to Walmart. The statement lands in a live debate. In January 2026, the advocacy group Groundwork argued that Google's agentic shopping standard could enable what it called a "surveillance pricing squeeze", a claim Google rejected as inaccurate on January 13. Walmart's text covers what the agent sees on Walmart.com; it does not address how offers are selected for an individual account.
The Walmart Agent Gateway
The gateway is a direct technical channel between agents and Walmart. According to the newsroom post, it "will give agents a faster, more reliable way to shop by using an MCP (model text protocol)."
That expansion is wrong. MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, the open standard for connecting AI models to external tools and data. The newsroom post does not explain the "model text protocol" wording, and the beta page does not use the acronym at all. The likeliest reading is a drafting error in the post, but Walmart has not said so.
Walmart says it will "begin with a beta for companies and developers." The Walmart.com page carries the same constraint in its footer: "Walmart Agent Gateway is an early beta program. Access is limited, available by invitation only, and may be suspended at any time." It adds that some features "may change and may not be available to all participants." The page has a "Request beta access" button but names no participating agent companies.
What the beta page adds
The undated landing page, headlined "Your AI agent shops better with Walmart," contains details absent from the newsroom post. The most significant is architectural: "Walmart Agent Gateway connects AI agents through Sparky for faster, more efficient & secure shopping." Outside agents, on this description, talk to Walmart's own assistant rather than to a raw product database. The newsroom post does not mention Sparky in connection with the gateway.
The page also lists four technical claims:
- "No more website scraping. Just up-to-date product & fulfillment data straight from the source."
- "Less waiting - reduce unnecessary requests, latency & token usage."
- "Built with verified identities, controlled permissions & observable actions for better security."
- "Walmart safeguards include category restrictions, rate limits & compliance guardrails for agents."
Neither document says which product categories are restricted, what the rate limits are, or how agent identity is verified. Token usage is a cost for the agent operator, not the shopper; Walmart's pitch on that line is aimed at the companies building agents.
Shopping for "usuals" without sharing history
One gateway feature addresses data exposure. According to Walmart, the gateway will help agents shop for a customer's usual items "without having to share their personal information or purchase history with the agent." The example given: if a customer tends to buy sourdough bread or a particular brand of milk, "Walmart will help the agent find those usual items for the customer without sharing the customer's broader shopping history."
The design keeps purchase history on Walmart's side of the connection. The agent asks; Walmart resolves the request against data the agent never receives. For Walmart, that keeps first-party purchase data, the raw material of its advertising business, inside its own systems.
Terms for AI agents
The third component is a rulebook. According to Walmart, the terms establish "what agents can and cannot do when shopping on behalf of a Walmart customer." The post lists eight points:
- Customers are in control, and Walmart's returns process applies, "including if an agent doesn't act as intended."
- Customers must approve agent purchases by default, and Walmart "may require additional approvals even for purchases within an agent's spending limits."
- Agents must not take actions beyond what the shopper intends.
- Agents do not receive customers' payment-card information and cannot add or change a customer's payment methods.
- Agents can access only the information needed for the task and allowed by the customer.
- The agent's privacy policy applies to information it receives; the agent provider handles what a customer shares with its app under its own policy.
- Walmart collects and processes information the agent provides under Walmart's Privacy Notice.
- "Agents that do not follow these terms will be blocked from Walmart's site."
Two of these carry weight beyond the obvious. The returns clause places the cost of agent mistakes on Walmart's standard returns process rather than leaving it unresolved between shopper and agent provider. The default-approval rule means the spending-limit option is something a customer has to switch on; out of the box, every agent purchase needs sign-off. Walmart also reserves the right to demand extra approval inside a limit, without saying when.
The privacy split is just as notable. Data flows in two directions, and each company keeps its own policy. What a customer tells an agent sits with the agent provider. What the agent passes to Walmart falls under Walmart's notice. Neither document explains how a customer would see what an agent has shared with Walmart.
The beta page links to a page titled "Agentic terms." The captured page does not show that document, and the newsroom post does not say when the terms take effect or how Walmart will detect an agent that breaks them.
Why this matters for marketers
The announcement arrives a month after Amazon took the opposite route with one of the most visible agents on the market. On September 20, Amazon cut Meta's Muse agent off from buying on Amazon.com, saying it never agreed to Muse operating on its store and that the agent did not identify itself. Walmart's post, by contrast, lists Muse among its existing conversational commerce integrations. Amazon's stance has a long history: in August 2025 it added six AI crawlers to its robots.txt file, and coverage at the time noted that Walmart and eBay had not blocked AI bots.
The legal backdrop shapes both approaches. On August 4, 2026, the Ninth Circuit vacated the injunction that had blocked Perplexity's Comet shopping agent from Amazon accounts, finding that the user, not the agent's developer, does the accessing. The court left retailers their contractual tools: terms of service, rate limiting and technical blocking. Walmart's announcement uses exactly those tools. It publishes terms, enforces them with blocking, and builds a sanctioned channel with rate limits.
Walmart's own record with agentic checkout explains the shape of the product. It was a launch partner for OpenAI's Instant Checkout in September 2025, and in March 2026 an executive said purchases inside ChatGPT converted three times worse than click-outs to Walmart's site. OpenAI shut Instant Checkout down that month, and Walmart moved to placing Sparky inside ChatGPT and later Gemini. The beta page's statement that the gateway "connects AI agents through Sparky" continues that strategy: third-party agents reach Walmart's catalogue through Walmart's assistant.
That has consequences for advertisers. Walmart Connect said in January that it was testing ad formats inside Sparky. If outside agents route through Sparky, the question of whether sponsored products surface in answers returned to an agent becomes relevant to every brand buying Walmart retail media. Neither document mentions advertising, sponsored listings or how product results are ranked for agents.
Walmart is also a co-developer of Google's UCP, the Universal Commerce Protocol published on January 11, 2026, which has built-in support for MCP. The same day, Walmart announced checkout inside Google's Gemini. A May scan by Originality.ai found only 26 sites with a public UCP file out of more than 3 million, and none on the primary domains of the named co-developers, Walmart included. The October 21 post does not mention UCP. How the gateway relates to Walmart's UCP and Gemini integrations is not explained.
Identity is the other open thread. The beta page promises "verified identities," a problem the industry has not solved. Arkose Labs reported on October 20 that only 2.3% of legitimate agent sessions carried verified Web Bot Auth signatures, according to Arkose's own platform data. HUMAN Security, also using its own data, said in September that Muse accounted for 72% of daily AI agent requests it observed. Walmart gives no figures on agent traffic to its own site.
What the documents do not say
Several practical details are missing from both sources:
- Which agent companies are in the gateway beta, and whether Muse, ChatGPT or Gemini will use it.
- Whether spending limits are per order or per period, and whether limits can vary by agent.
- When the agent terms take effect, and whether agents already shopping through browsers must move to the gateway.
- How Walmart will detect and block non-compliant agents.
- Which product categories are restricted for agents.
- Whether Agent Profiles reach Sam's Club accounts at the same time as Walmart accounts.
The Walmart.com page has no visible date. Its content matches the October 21 newsroom post and it carries a "View blog" link, but the capture shows no publication or update date.

Summary
Who: Walmart, for customers of Walmart and Sam's Club and for the companies and developers that build AI shopping agents.
What: Three components for agent shopping. Agent Profiles give each agent its own profile inside a customer's account, with separate purchase history, per-purchase approval by default and optional spending limits such as $50, $100 or $200. The Walmart Agent Gateway is a direct channel for agents, described as MCP-based and, on Walmart.com, as routed through Sparky. Terms for AI agents bar access to payment-card data, require purchases to stay within the shopper's intent, apply Walmart's returns process to agent mistakes and threaten blocking for agents that break the rules.
When: Announced on October 21, 2026. Agent Profiles are due "in the next month." The gateway starts as an invitation-only beta; the Walmart.com beta page is undated.
Where: Walmart.com and Sam's Club, through agents and apps chosen by customers. The announcement does not name markets beyond Walmart's US sites.
Why: According to Walmart, agents currently sign in with customers' credentials, so their purchases cannot be told apart, and browser-based shopping is slow and error-prone for software. The move also comes as Amazon blocks unsanctioned agents and courts leave retailers with contractual tools rather than computer-crime claims, giving Walmart a path to admit agents on its own terms while keeping purchase history on its side of the connection.
